Some years ago a great deal of American silver was circulated in Canada and there were many reasons why that was not very desirable. One reason was that these American coins were displacing our own silver on which we made a profit. Steps were taken to collect that silver through the banks and ship it away. The result was that for some years we have had little or no American silver in Canada. I think that is quite important. There is not the same inducement to-day for shipping it away, hut I would ask my hon. friend whether the banks still continue to export American silver under the arrangement with the Finance Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We stopped paying the banks anything for that about eighteen months ago in view of the shortness of our own silver. When we return to normal conditions the former practice will again be adopted.

Under the Gresham law poorer money always drives out the better, and almost as a matter of economics the American importations have been leaving Canada and finding their way over to the United States.

I would like to ask another question with respect to the new one-cent pieces which were provided for in a measure passed last year and which were to be much smaller in size than those now in circulation. I know the minister does not deal very much with these coins, but to me, and to a good many of my colleagues this coinage is a matter of some importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Possibly my pocket has been worn out by the large Canadian cent just as much as the pocket of my hon. friend. It is a coin I am very familiar with bearing in mind what the salaries of Cabinet Ministers are. However, the character of the coin is settled. The orders were given a long time ago for the necessary dies from Great Britain, but they are not here yet. We are doing the best we can to get them, and as soon as they reach here I do not think more than forty-eight hours will elapse before we will be turning out those one-cent pieces.
Resolution reported.
Sir HENRY DRAYTON (Minister of Finance) thereupon moved for leave to introduce BBl No. 15, to amend the Currency Act, IbiO.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE OF BOTH HOUSES ON UNIFICATION OF CERTAIN BRANCHES.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: JOINT COMMITTEE OF BOTH HOUSES ON UNIFICATION OF CERTAIN BRANCHES.
speechtext: I have the honour to inform the House that a message has been received from the Senate requesting this House to unite with the Senate in the appointment of a Joint Committee consisting of an equal number of members of both Houses to consider and report upon the desirability of uniting certain branches of the two Houses performing similar duties and particularly the Law Branch, the Law Translation Branch, and the Debates Translation Branch, and, if in the opinion of the committee, it is desirable to unite any of the branches, to submit a scheme therefor, and that the Honourable Messieurs Bel-eourt, Dandurand, Dennis, Foster, Fowler, Sharpe and Thompson be appointed as members of such committee to act on behalf of the Senate. .

On motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That tt is expedient to amend the Government Annuities Act, 1908, and to provide (a) for the sale of annuities to any person resident in Canada; (b) for the increase of the total amount which may be paid by way of an annuity or annuities to an annuitant or to joint annuitants from $1,000 to $5,000 a year; and (c) for the increase of the rate of interest from three to four per cent per annum payable on moneys repaid to the purchaser or his legal representatives when the annuitant or the last survivor of joint annuitants dies before the annuity becomes payable and moneys have been paid or deposited as consideration for the annuity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the object of this resolution and the legislation to be based upon it is to make Government annuities more popular than they are at present, to stimulate public interest in them, and to raise larger sums of money than have been raised in the past under the Government Annuities Act. The changes proposed are not very great, but they are considered necessary by the department having the matter in charge in order to make possible a greater sale of the annuities, in the interest not only of the country but also of those who purchase them.
The first change is to provide that annuities may be sold to any person resident in Canada. The department desires to be in a position to sell annuities to any one in Canada; they do not want to be confined to selling them only to persons who can

prove domicile in this country. That is merely in the direction of removing a barrier which has stood in the way of selling these annuities.
The original intention in connection with the sale of annuities by the Government was to provide for an income to the annuitant of comparatively small amount. Of course, the first idea of the annuity was that it was entirely for the benefit of the annuitant, not of the country. That idea has long since been exploded, at any rate in so far as matters on this side of the Atlantic are concerned. The large insurance companies have gone very extensively into the business of selling annuities and in this connection are making very large sums of money. The sale of annuities ought to be a good thing for the Government; it is a transaction in connection with which the country ought to receive a large amount of money. If it pays ordinary commercial companies to sell annuities, it ought to pay, and I have no doubt will pay the country to sell them. Now, the total amount payable yearly by way of annuity has-been $1,000; the department have requested that the amount be increased to $5,000 so that they may be enabled to do business with individual or joint annuitants to the extent of that amount.
Then there is the matter of the age at which annuities may be drawn. Under the present law no one can obtain payments under an annuity until he has become fifty-five years of age. That again limits the field in which annuities may be sold; and there would seem to be no reason for the restriction. The insurance companies do not impose any such restriction; they charge more, just as the Government would charge more for annuities payable a* an earlier age. The profit obtained in connection with the sale of annuities which become payable at forty or forty-five when the charge is based upon a proper table of rates is just as good as that obtained in connection with the sale of annuities payable at fifty-five. The department, therefore, ask that that barrier also be removed.
The fourth matter covered by the resolution, that of providing for an increase of the rate of interest from three to four per cent per annum payable on moneys repaid to the purchaser or his legal representatives when the annuitant dies before the annuity becomes payable, is an important one. There are different kinds of annuities. There are guaranteed annuities, in connection with which a certain number of annual 26J
payments are payable after the annuity becomes payable whether the annuitant is alive or not. Then you have an annuity issued at a much lower rate under which the annuitant, if he dies before the date on which the annuity becomes payable, loses everything he has paid. Then you have an intermediate class which falls short of the guaranteed payment of annuities but which is entitled to a return of moneys paid with interest at three per cent. This intermediate class offers a two-fold inducement: It encourages savings and it guarantees their return with interest in case the annuitant dies before he attains the age at which the annuity is to commence. Now, at the time this rate of three per cent was fixed, money was a great deal cheaper than it is now, and the department says that in order to make effective any argument regarding the benefit of annuities from the standpoint of savings the interest rate should be four instead of three per cent.
Would this apply to annuities that have been issued already?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, this would not necessarily apply to any existing contract. All annuities turn upon contract.

The objects of those who devised the original annuity scheme are not quite the same as those of the Minister of Finance, The original scheme was devised for the benefit of the annuitants, whereas my hon. friend is devising a scheme for the benefit and convenience of the Government. He wants to draw more money into the public treasury, and I suppose no objection can be taken to that, because he needs it badly This Bill is designed, not for the benefit of the annuitant, but to get more money into the public treasury. It was never intended that this should be a scheme to compete with insurance companies. Inasmuch as it was a privilege that was granted, it was not considered necessary to give it to everybody. But I do not think any harm can come from extending it as my hon. friend suggests. Then it was intended that the annuitant should receive a moderate sum; I do not think it was intended that he should get $5,000; I think the original sum was $600-at all events, the sum was a small one. The scheme was never intended as one to compete with insurance companies, but to meet the case of many simple people who did not understand insurance, who had great faith in the Government and who would take up a Govern-

ment scheme when they might not take up an insurance scheme. Theiefore, it was not intended to be a scheme to pay large annuities. My hon. friend is now going into competition with insurance companies. I do not know that any great harm can come from that, but it is quite evident that his viewpoint is not quite the same as that of the former minister who devised the scheme. No exception can be taken to the increase in interest in a given case. Money is worth more than in former times. Out of that, however, a suggestion arises, that I perhaps do not want to press too strongly. It seems. to me that the argument that is used in favour of an increased rate of interest might also apply to an increased rate of interest on savings bank deposits. The rate of interest on savings bank deposits ought not, I grant, to be changed frequently. If you increase it, you cannot very easily take it down; and. if there were a temporary hardness of the money market which would seem to make money dearer, I should not think that would be a reason why the interest on savings bank deposits should be increased. But where you have a continued condition running for years with a high interest value for money, I think the question of the rate of interest in the savings bank presents itself in a stronger light than in former times. I remember one occasion when a strong argument was put up to increase the rate of interest in the savings bank. I did not concur in the suggestion; but as a compromise I said this: We will create a Government stock of 31 per cent, and if the people who have money in the savings bank attach sufficient importance to getting the higher rate, they can convert their savings bank deposits into 3i per cent stock. I did not expect that very many would do that, and as a matter of fact very few did it. People who put money in the savings bank are of a class that does not understand finance; the question of rate of interest is not a very serious matter to them; what they want to know is that the money is there; that the Government is behind it, and they can get their money when they want it. I do not know, if my hon. friend were to* increase the rate of interest on savings bank deposits, whether he would get much thanks for doing so. In the face of present conditions, however, where you have had a long period of years during which money has been getting dearer, and it is probably going to be dearer next year than this year, the minister might consider ]Mr. Fielding. [
whether he would not be justified in increasing the savings bank rate.
There is another point. My hon. friend has intimated that the Government want to make this annuity system more popular. I do not know whether he has at hand any evidence to show to what extent people have taken advantage of this annuity scheme, but I think he is quite correct in implying that it is not very popular. I do not wish to introduce a note of complaint regarding his predecessor, but what happened was this. When this annuity scheme was devised, it was realized by its promoters that it was like insurance; that it was a good thing, but that people do not usually take out insurance until somebody goes to them and explains the matter-canvasses them. I suppose nearly three out of four members of this House will confess that their first insurance policies were taken out, not because they had the economic law in mind, but because some clever agent came and put the proposition before them. So we realized that if we expected to make this annuity scheme a success, we would have to do something to advertise it; that we would have to send men into the field to explain it, and we accordingly appointed a number of lecturers-I think they were called, agents,-canvassers to do that service. In the year 1911 a remarkable event happened
A sad event.

-and a change of Government occurred. The Government that came into power decided that those lecturers were not necessary; that they were not any good, and the Government quietly dispensed with their services. Of course, it so happened that those lecturers had been appointed by a Liberal Government, and, perhaps, it would be wrong to suggest that that had anything to do with their services being dispensed with, but still the fact remains that the services of those lecturers, who were to be the canvassers to make this scheme successful, were dispensed with. We were told that the Government were going to substitute for that a better system; that they were going to make the postmasters of the country agents; that the postmasters were to give all the information. Soon after that information had been given out in the public press, I was in a large important town, a shire town down East-I shall not mention the name. I went to the postmaster, and I said:	"I
want information about the annuity scheme." He said:	"What"? I said:
"The annuity scheme." He said: "What

annuity scheme "? Well, I gave him a little outline of what it was, and I said that it had been announced by the Government in the public press and otherwise that this scheme was to be carried out by the postmasters, and I said: " I suppose you have some instructions in regard to the matter." He said: "I suppose I have." He agreed to look for instructions, and a day or two afterwards when I asked him about them, he said that he supposed they had come, but he could not find them. It is not surprising under those conditions that the annuity scheme proved a failure. I do not know what method my hon. friend has in mind of putting the information before the public; but I would strongly advise him, even at the risk of not having Liberal appointees, to adopt the principle of the insurance companies and to send somebody amongst the people to explain the whole scheme to them, and then he will not have to come before the House and say that the scheme is a failure.

The conversation to
which we have just listened as well as we could at this end of the room is very interesting to me as illustrating how careful Governments should be in taking up business that on the whole would be just as well-or in nine cases out of ten better- done by private individuals. I notice the original Act dates back from the year 1908, and I am pretty sure that if I had been in the House then I would have protested against the original Act, although I would have been a very young member, on the ground that it is not desirable on general grounds that the Government of a great country like this should undertake business which is being done by private individuals. I think that general ground is a sound ground. This is just another example of that system of paternalism which is proving such an attraction to the comparatively limited population of a country like Canada. The worse fault that is taking hold of people to-day, so far as I can see, is that everybody wants to be governing his neighbour; people have a passion for looking after other people, and by means of the Government. I endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. - Fielding) as to the original intention of this Act, and I must say that I listened almost aghast to the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) in so far as those remarks showed that, with a lightness of heart, he was prepared to embark upon a scheme of money-making on behalf of this Government, in the conduct of a business which, I repeat, is properly the business of insurance societies.
Where are we going to end if these ideas of the functions of a Government are to prevail on both sides and in all corners of this House? We shall end in the buildnig up ' of a top-heavy bureaucracy, that is where we shall end. Men of all political persuasions are telling our people that what this country needs at the present time is production, and any one who knows Canada knows that there is an ample field for the activities of individuals in almost any line of human endeavour. There is an ample field for individualistic enterprise, and that is what the country wants-individual effort, for their own sakes in the first place, and to the certain advantage of the country in the second place. If you keep on extending the sphere of governmental action you inevitably keep on increasing the number of your civil servants. We are told we have far too many already, and that we ought to economize by carefully reducing their numbers, and certainly by being most careful in making new appointments. I think that is so, but if every second man you meet from the Atlantic to the Pacific is seeking for a Government job, without any regard to the preaching of annuities or anything else, how are you going to increase your production? I want just in a sentence or two to warn my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) against letting this idea of Government go too far with him. I am charmed with his first appearances in this House. His powers of exposition are great, but his political experience is brief, and I hope he will consult very frequently the Acting Prime Minister before he gives out such novel, radical, and I had almost said, Bolshevist doctrines. I suppose if we had a Soviet form of Government, everything would be in the hands of the Government, but I do think on the whole that annuities would be better handled by insurance companies than by any government that I can conceive of or have seen in Canada hitherto.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that I am very, very open to instruction in politics in every direction. I know I can get a lot of information from my hon. friend, and I hope he will be kind enough to give it to me from time to time. But with reference to this particular matter I really had the idea that Government annuities were supposed to be a good thing, and1 that they were not at all novel. My idea, I think, is not very far from the truth. Certainly I do not desire to have an army of

men trying to sell Government annuities. My opinion is that the Government annuity business should be either stopped entirely or put upon such a basis as will recommend itself to the people whom we are asking to invest in them. Every one will agree that thd original idea of Government annuities was to help the people who bought them. But {hey do not help if the terms are such that it does not pay any one to take them out. Annuities were surely never intended to be issued upon a basis that would give the Government an infinitely greater return that it had a right to get. They were established for the purpose of encouraging and helping people to save. Of course, we need production in this country, but we also need saving, and probably need it almost as much as production. Production and saving ought to go side-by side, but you are not going to help saving by offering only 3 per cent. We may, and I hope we will, get people to save by making the changes I have suggested.
Resolution reported.
Sir HENRY DRAYTON thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 16, to amend the Government Annuities Act, 1908.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

On the motion of Hon. C. C. Ballantyne (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), for the House to go into Committee on the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to repeal sections eighty-five to eighty-nine, both inclusive, and section ninety-one of the Canada Shipping Act, chapter one hundred and thirteen of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, and to reenact in lieu thereof:

1.	That every British subject who,-
(a)	served as a master or mate of a seagoing or coasting sailing vessel of over seventy-five tons, gross tonnage, before the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and twenty, for a full period of twelve months within ten years immediately next preceding the date of his application for certificate of service,
(b)	produces satisfactory evidence of his sobriety, experience, ability and general good conduct on board ship, and
(c)	passes the sight test and the prescribed examination in signalling, shall be entitled, on payment of the prescribed fee, to a certificate of service as a master or mate of a square rigged or fore-and-aft rigged sea-going or coasting sailing vessel not exceeding seven hundred and fifty tons, registered tonnage, according as his service has been (a) as master or as mate, (b) on a sea-going or on a coasting sailing vessel, (c) on a square rigged sailing ship or on a fore-and-aft rigged sailing vessel.
[Sit Henry Drayton.]
2.	That in every such certificate of service the name, place and date of birth of the person to whom the same is issued shall be stated, and each certificate shall specify whether the holder is entitled to act as master or mate, whether the certificate is for seagoing vessels or for vessels in the coasting trade, and whether for square rigged sailing vessels or for fore-and-aft sailing vessels, and that it is not for any vessel exceeding seven hundred and fifty tons, registered tonnage.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I presume that this is the proper time to discuss the principle of this resolution. Legislation very much akin to what is aimed at by this resolution was introduced in the latter part of one of the sessions last year by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), but it met with such vigorous opposition from hon. members, including myself, that the minister thought proper to withdraw the Bill. Now the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) comes forward with a resolution, not exactly word for word, but on almost precisely the same lines as the legislation introduced by the hon. member for Halifax last year. We all know that a certain standard oh education, experience and ability is required of professional men in this country. In the case of lawyers, doctors, engineers, or any other professional men,	certain	educational	requirementshave to be met, and certain experience must have been had before they are permitted to practice. I venture to say that captaincy and charge of ships has been regarded not merely as a profession in this country, but as a very honourable and very onerous profession for the last hundred years and more. The Minister of Marine and	Fisheries	now	brings	before thisParliament legislation that would do away entirely with educational requirements in the	case	of a	man whoseduty	it is to	take	charge	of a ship.
According to this resolution, if a man obtained a certificate ten years ago stating that he had served on board ship for twelve months somewhere in Canada, now, after the lapse of that time during which he may have done anything else and may have forgotten all about seamanship, he can claim a license as a captain qualified to put to sea with a crew. The sections in Chapter 113 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, (Sections 85 to 89 inclusive, are very simple in their requirements and are not, I think, too exacting. If this proposed legislation were restricted to coasting vessels there would not be so much danger. But it is also contemplated to license such

men as I have mentioned to go across the ocean. What would happen to such a captain if he went to Liverpool? He might take his ship there but he would never be able to leave, because his certificate would be regarded as a taere "scrap of paper." He would have to show a certificate recognized on the other side by the Board of Trade. It is possible that the minister may have consulted the English Board of Trade and obtained their approval of this Bill. If he has not done so, I fear that the captains who may possess these unsatisfactory certificates will find themselves in difficulty in the Old Country. We know of instances in which engineeis have gone from Canada to the Old Country with certificates that were good enough here but were rejected on the other side, and in this predicament competent engineers had to be secuied to clear the ships from the ports in England. I earnestly submit that in order to take charge of an ocean vessel a man must have adequate knowledge of seafaring and be able to ascertain his position by the use of the proper instruments. So far as I am concerned, I desire it to be distinctly understood that I repudiate any responsibility that might accrue by the enacting of such legislation as this, for I think it is a most dangerous thing to put life and property in the hands of incompetent captains. The insurance companies of this country, I think, would lefuse to insure ships or cargoes intended to be sent to sea under the control of men who were palpably incompetent in every sense, at least in the matter of training. The minister was not in the House when the Bill to which I have made reference was introduced. If he had been he would recall that both our own law and the English law on the subject were cited, and that after due consideration of the facts the hon. member who introduced the Bill deemed it wise to withdraw it. I am therefore surprised that within such a short time the minister should seek to establish such a low standard of seamanship in this country. In conclusion, I can only emphasize my protest and leave the responsibility entirely with the minister and those who may be disposed to implement this resolution by an Act of Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I was not present
at the special session of the House when the then acting minister introduced the Bill in question, which was not similar to, but different from this. That Bill applied to sailing vessels propelled by auxiliary
power, but this resolution does not apply to such vessels. It applies only to " sailing vessels," of a certain tonnage. Under the Shipping Act any master who served on a sailing vessel prior to 1870, if he were alive to-day, and were sober, experienced and of adequate ability and general good conduct, would be entitled to a certificate on the payment of the prescribed fee. The hon. member will at once realize that we could not expect men to be fit captains of sailing ships who had served prior to the year 1870, and this resolution seeks to repeal Section 85 of the Shipping Act, and to enact that any man who has served on a sailing vessel for twelve months within the past ten years and possesses the qualifications to which I have referred, in addition to a knowledge of signalling, shall be granted a service certificate. This is nothing new. We are merely bringing the Shipping Act up to date, and it is difficult for me to apprehend the reasoning of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) in his argument that the legislation proposed is unusual and hazardous.
I wish to say to the hon. member that the service certificate that shall be granted to an officer who desires to become a master of a sailing ship, should this resolution and the Bill that is to be based upon it pass, is a service certificate that will be recognized just th same as a competency certificate. There is absolutely no difference so far as recognition by the English authorities is concerned between the service certificate and the competency certificate.
With regard to the other clause, I wish to have section 86 of the Act repealed also because a mate cannot obtain a service certificate without going back as far as 1883. Surely hon. members will not object to the changes that the resolution calls for in order that both a master and a mate, instead of having to go back to 1870 for the master and 1883 for the mate, may, upon a service of ten years be capable of obtaining a service certificate. During the last few years captains and mates of sailing vessels have become very scarce; in fact; they were so difficult to get that during the war I had to take the necessary authority under the War Measures Act to grant service certificates to masters and mates of sailing vessels. My object in bringing forward this resolution now is to meet the absolute necessity that exists for more masters and mates by enabling them to get service certificates for sailing ships. The Act introduced at the special session

of the House was for sailing ships driven by auxiliary power. This resolution is confined to sailing craft only. There is another section of the Shipping Act-section 87-that I desire to have repealed. It provides that a vessel shall be only 100 registered tons and not over 150. The resolution stipulates that the tonnage may be increased to 750 tons. My hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) comes from a maritime province, and I am sure that he appreciates better than I do the fact that those experienced men who have been on sailing ships for a number of years, while they may not be able, owing to Jack of education to pass the competency test and therefore obtain competency certificates, are just as good men and just as competent, providing that their eyesight is all right and that they understand signalling, as others who may be better equipped as far as education goes. But we cannot put men on sailing vessels who are seventy years of age. I therefore wish to repeal the clause so as to provide that masters and mates who have served, within the past ten years, for twelve months on board a sailing ship may be granted a certificate providing they have the qualifications that I have referred to.

If it is agreeable to the House I would move that we adjourn at six o'clock, but I would like, before we do that, to take Private Bills so as to get them one stage farther ahead.
